doors.label: Tax cap
doors.sentence: Voted YES on the 7 May 2026 budget — 7.28% overall, 9.34% residential, 4.78% business — the fourth consecutive above-inflation increase after 6.15%, 7.93% and 6.99%. Police are 69.5% of the increase ($78.05M). The campaign site has no tax or budget plank of any kind, and no located sentence names a cap, a formula or a ceiling.

doors.label: Downtown order
doors.sentence: “we're gradually enforcing city bylaws that authorities have ignored for decades.” Beside it, her own costed breakdown: “$3.6 million for bylaw and community safety hubs, and $2 million for additional police officers.” Delivered: hubs at 999 Pandora and 709 Douglas, a third funded at Burnside Gorge, 10 Community Safety and Bylaw officers, a 7-officer VicPD Beat Team. No unified Public Order Team, no bylaw-hours position, no published weekly dashboard.

doors.label: Housing
doors.sentence: “The housing stuff has to keep going.” Campaign site: “Our community deserves housing that's secure, affordable and built to last.” Record beside it: 2,359 net new occupancies at the two-year mark against a 4,902 five-year target, and 363 below-market rentals against a 1,798 five-year target. No unit target, no 25/20/15 mix, no vacancy target.

doors.label: Written program
doors.sentence: A campaign site exists and the platform does not. Under each of the three policy headings on electalto.ca/policies sits the line “Check back later for the full platform release!” — with nominations open 1–11 Sep and the vote on 17 Oct. No questionnaire answers anywhere: Livable CRD lists her as an incumbent with all nine category cells blank (responses due 18 Sep); VoteMate says “this candidate hasn't added promises to VoteMate.” Her only substantive 2026 policy writing is one op-ed, 16 Aug 2026.

cells.quote: The housing stuff has to keep going.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: the OCP “Villages and Corridors” (adopted 2 Oct 2025) and Missing Middle (YES 26 Jan 2023) are zoning levers doing M6's work, against M6's composition targets plus quarterly reporting. Same-week context: “we have to put some intentionality behind it and that's all about the official community plan.” Capped below Close by a sourced miss: 363 below-market rentals against a 1,798 five-year target, and 61 Missing Middle permits in 2024 against 150/yr. Campaign site adds only a theme — “housing that's secure, affordable and built to last” — with no unit target and no 25/20/15 mix.

cells.quote: This project shows what's possible when local and provincial governments and community partners come together” — *Wellness House, 938 Mason St: the City contributed $262,500 from the Housing Reserve Fund \plus the land** for 34 units of culturally supportive housing run by the Aboriginal Coalition to End Homelessness.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: a City-land disposition to a non-profit Indigenous housing partner is the outcome M6b describes, done case by case. Also $677,500 to the 179-unit Tresah West co-op, 16 Apr 2026. Capped below Close by a sourced miss: her own 2022 platform promised “Create a city land bank program” and no parcel-level public inventory, acquisition fund, competitive disposition policy or standing right of first refusal exists • after four years.

cells.quote: City launched “Virtual Assistant Vic”, Permit Finder and expanded eApply under the federally funded Development Process Review, 6 Jul 2026; Development Fee Waiver Bylaw in force 29 Jan 2026.
cells.why: No mayor quote in either release, and no processing-time figures, targets or performance metrics published at all — which is the whole of M7. No AI pre-screening of applications. Reporter paraphrase that “the city streamlined its approvals process” is not her mouth and is not the instrument.

cells.quote: Named YES, 8–1, on the DCC grant/waiver for below-market housing providers ($1.8M/yr, Housing Accelerator Fund), Nov 2024.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: M8's DCC lever, applied to non-market rather than purpose-built rental, with no published infrastructure funding plan beside it. Supporting record: parking minimums reduced 6–3 (31 Aug 2025); March 2025 OCP package reduced ACCs for affordable homeownership 7–2 and setbacks 6–2, Alto never among the named opposed. No 5% vacancy target and no suite amnesty — two of the three legs are silent. Context: Greater Victoria vacancy reached 3.3%, highest since 1999 (Dec 2025).

cells.quote: The important thing about them being located in those two places is that they bring a visibility, a presence, an acknowledgement that those two areas right now require some concentrated services.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: community safety field hubs at 999 Pandora and 709 Douglas, $3.6M for “bylaw and community safety hubs” on her own campaign accounting, $250K moved for a third at Burnside Gorge, 10 Community Safety and Bylaw officers and a 7-officer VicPD Beat Team plus 2 supporting bylaw — co-location and joint deployment against M26's single unified operation. Neither the unified command with an 8 AM briefing and one field supervisor, nor the weekly DPOT dashboard, exists.

cells.quote: The 2022 platform listed “community crisis response teams” under Well Being — Record for an incumbent, never Plan.
cells.why: No 2026 sentence anywhere, including the safety op-ed, and no civilian crisis response capacity, published dispatch criteria or diversion figure. The op-ed's own framing cuts against it: “Municipal government does not control housing, health care, social services, addictions treatment or income support.”

cells.quote: Council reallocated $10.35M to Community Safety and Wellbeing actions including 12 additional bylaw staff (<$1.9M), 2 Jul 2025; 10 officers reported hired by 2026; $3.6M cited by her for bylaw and hubs.
cells.why: Headcount and money, never hours — no 6am–10pm 7-day position, no published deployment pattern, and no funding-source rule. Contradicts no 2026 promise, so shown and not scored.

cells.quote: we're gradually enforcing city bylaws that authorities have ignored for decades.
cells.why: Commits × same instrument — M33 is “we don't need new laws, we need to enforce the ones we have”, and this is that sentence, in her own 2026 campaign writing. Record supports: named YES 8–1 on the daytime-sheltering motion, 18 Jul 2024 (“do more, do it better, do it faster”), and YES 7–2 on the 2025 parks bylaw with a 34-park positive list and tents limited to overhead cover. Capped below Close by a sourced miss: staff priced full daytime enforcement on Pandora, streets and parks at $4.7M/yr and it was not funded. Her own caveat: “We cannot move people unless we have someplace for them to go.”

cells.what: drug-use buffer (City: list + bylaw/DPOT + VicPD/CDSA; not City seizure)
cells.quote: The 2025 parks bylaw set a 15-metre separation from playgrounds, adopted 7–2 with Alto in the majority — a child-focused-space setback, but applied to sheltering, not drug use.
cells.why: Adjacency is not a source, so shown and not scored. Her 2026 vote against the motion to close the supervised consumption site (failed 1–8, 2 Jul 2026) is not scored either: the Program proposes no such closure. No protected list, no posted sites, no CDSA coordination statement.

cells.quote: The ultimate goal is for the block to remain accessible to everyone who needs to be there,” and “This is an annual deeper clean than our regular maintenance, and so this is the third year that we've done this.
cells.why: Commits × neither: a 900-block Pandora closure and clean in its third year is an annual operation, not any of the cluster's instruments — not same-day removal of obstructing structures with a 30–60 minute compliance window (M34), not the capacity-first 5 PM shelter publication (M35), not permanent visible patrols in named spaces (M36), not all-night lighting (M37).

cells.what: tax glide path (capped on the residential rate)
cells.quote: Voting for the budget were councillors Matt Dell, Jeremy Caradonna, Chris Coleman, Dave Thompson, Krista Loughton and Mayor Marianne Alto.” Adopted 7.28% overall / 9.34% residential / 4.78% business, 7 May 2026 — against M66's Year-1 residential cap of 6.5%.
cells.why: Disagrees: a named vote setting the residential rate, which is the exact object of the measure. Fourth consecutive above-inflation increase (6.15%, 7.93%, 6.99%, 7.28%); $394.1M operating, $160.1M capital; police 69.5% of the increase. Her nearest 2026 sentence — “We're trying to find that sweet spot between what we have to do, what we'd like to do, and what people can afford to pay for” — raises the topic with no goal and no instrument: a Mention, which does not lift the mark. The campaign site has no tax plank. Distinct from the 3 Mar reserve motion on row 14.

cells.quote: A motion put forward by the mayor to reduce contributions to the reserve funds ultimately passed.” She proposed four reductions: eliminate the debt-reduction reserve contribution, eliminate the parking services/infrastructure allocation, cut vehicles and heavy equipment to $2.25M, cut corporate contingency to $400,000 — $5.5M applied to lowering the tax increase. Alto: “there is no doubt at all that we're handing the next council a significant challenge” and “These costs don't go away, they're simply put aside for the future consideration of the next council.
cells.why: Disagrees: M66c exists precisely to make the scheduled debt-reduction contribution unavailable as a balancing item. No over-collection refund rule (M66b), no published debt-outstanding, debt-service or debt-per-household metrics.

cells.quote: We're hopeful that the discussions that we've had today will continue to urge the provincial government to pay their share of all these costs,” and “we expect the government to come to the table repeatedly. And at some point we will want a cheque or two.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: she co-chairs and convenes the mayors' caucus day at the legislature on the largest communities' shared files, doing the work of M70b's twice-yearly formal advocacy. Op-ed reinforces the jurisdictional line: “Municipal government does not control housing, health care, social services, addictions treatment or income support.” No quarterly downloading ledger with a cost per file, and no published refusal threshold — the half that would make it Aligned. Separate source and date from row 13, so “filling gaps because other orders of government are not doing their job” is context here, not the mark.

cells.what: CRD cost and the Goldstream plant
business, downtown, one mandate not a new office
cells.quote: Local businesses are essential to Victoria's economy and to the wellbeing and vitality of our neighbourhoods. By listening to the business community, we're removing barriers and making City services work better for businesses.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: a business-licence process review, a Business Experience Survey and quarterly economic reporting, against M72's 5-business-day licence standard and M71's quarterly vacancy report. Also Launch Victoria with the Chamber (7 Aug 2026) and patio fees held at 2026 levels with CPI indexing instead of doubling. Campaign site adds “smart investments in businesses and the economy, a vibrant downtown core, and year-round events.” No 11%→5% vacancy target, no single named mandate, no published Strategic Economic Plan, no Conference Centre net-cost number.

cells.what: capital threshold, short-stay parking (15-min grace; first-hour gated Year 2), permit fees
cells.quote: Development Fee Waiver Bylaw in force 29 Jan 2026 – 29 Jan 2027, waiving rezoning, development permit, public hearing and community meeting fees for a year — a fee instrument, but on development applications rather than M76's under-$50K homeowner work, and no mayor quote in the release. No $25M capital-approval threshold, no 15-minute grace, no short-stay parking instrument. 2022 leftover “curb management strategy” unused as Plan.

cells.what: Host Nations Foundation. Topic never drops out of the 12. A dash is still allowed on M1–M5.
cells.quote: The City is honoured to continue its partnership with the Songhees Nation and to financially support this significant celebration and recognition of Indigenous resiliency and culture.
cells.why: Commits × neither: City money and a continuing partnership, but none of the five instruments — no quarterly government-to-government table with published summaries (M1); the Purchasing Policy, revised July 2024, contains no Indigenous procurement provisions at all (M2); no lək̓ʷəŋən dual-naming programme in this term — the səʔit Street renaming was adopted 23 Jun 2022, before she was mayor (M3); no protocol package developed with the Nations (M4); no urban Indigenous services liaison position (M5). Context: City Family (est. 2017), Reconciliation Contribution Fund (est. 2022), $200K annual Nations grant since the 2023 budget, and Wellness House. Chair and City Family roles are a seat held, not a source.

cells.what: tenant protections, STR, indoor heat (M9c struck; 26°C gated)
cells.quote: Tenant Protection During Redevelopment Bylaw No. 25-044 adopted under her chairmanship (2025), following the 7–2 direction of 15 May 2025 to study higher compensation for displaced tenants — she called the amended version “better than nothing”; a further renter-protections motion passed unanimously 29 May 2026. Plus “This is absolutely an investment in prevention” — $100K added to the rent bank in the budget package she moved.
cells.why: Commits × same instrument on M9 (a demoviction bylaw is exactly M9's notice/compensation/right-of-return vehicle). Capped below Close by a sourced action the other way: she moved to have the Province delay the short-term-rental principal-residence ban, arguing STRs “have provided an alternative accommodation option for the tourism sector, complementing the hotel and motel industry” (Mar 2024) — the opposite direction to M9b. No indoor-heat position. M9c struck — not scored.

cells.quote: Our partnership with The Salvation Army expands much-needed emergency shelter beds in the community and supports their STEP program's sober-living, substance-free approach” — 13 beds, City $310K to 31 Mar 2028 — and, in her own campaign accounting, “$5.4 million for community supports, shelter spaces, housing, and emergency weather response.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: funded shelter-to-housing pathways against M11's Housing First plus a STEP-style throughput programme. No published throughput, no cost per successful placement, no returns-within-12-months figure, no unsheltered-count target. Her regional fair-share position — “We do not have room for anyone else… We think we've done enough”, and in the op-ed “Victoria cannot be the only answer to challenges that belong to the whole region” — is consistent with the Program's own demand on the other 12 municipalities and is not a second mark.

cells.what: childcare, doctors, youth (M13 school food is $0 → M13d)
cells.quote: Local organizations are experiencing unprecedented demand for their programs and services to support at-risk children, youth and families. This funding helps activate the prevention and intervention aspects of the City's Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan.” — $750K from Public Safety Canada's Crime Prevention Action Fund, 16 partners, 19 projects.
cells.why: Commits × neither: grant pass-through is none of the cluster's instruments. Strong Record context that does not lift a word mark: council adopted childcare in all zones except industrial with staff-level permit approval, 14 Sep 2023 — that is M12's pre-zoning lever, but no tally and no Alto quote exist for it; the $630K Youth Bus Pass was retained in the 2026 budget, which is M13c's fare instrument; and her M13b position — “permissive tax exemptions for not-for-profit health societies and clinics” — is 2022 text, Record only.

cells.quote: Her own motion, 21 May 2025, echoing Esquimalt's call for SD61 trustee electoral reform (ward-based rather than at-large), after the Province dismissed all nine trustees in January 2025 and appointed a sole trustee.
cells.why: No tally reported. That is board governance, not M13d's instrument — no standing joint agreement, no published annual work plan, no annual joint public meeting, no joint-use facilities agreement, no safe-routes-to-school programme. Adjacency is not a source, so shown and not scored.

cells.quote: $4.4 million for extra sanitation and capital improvements to streetscape and public realm related to safety and wellbeing” — her own campaign accounting.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: the funded instrument behind it is council action #4, “Increase public works attention to Pandora, Princess, and downtown” (<$390,000), which does M17's work (downtown sweeping and bin service) without M17's daily standard or evening and weekend hours. No 90%-graffiti-in-48-hours published service standard (M14) — the City's 2025 graffiti spend was ≈$604K across three departments with no response-time target; no pest-management plan (M16) — Hammond's rodent motion carried unanimously with Alto not individually quoted; no murals-instead-of-graffiti expansion (M18) beyond the standing $150K public art budget. This sentence carries the mark here only; it is context on rows 6 and 23.

cells.what: mobility + Vision Zero (M39 30 km/h struck; calming is M38)
cells.quote: Improving safety and accessibility is one of the most important investments we can make to support community wellbeing. These upgrades will create more comfortable options for everyone while maintaining our roads and helping us build a safer and more reliable transportation network.” — Blanshard and Cook corridor works, incl. a new signal at Blanshard/Pembroke; 2026–27 programme extends to Pandora (Cook–Fort) and Begbie–Shelbourne.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: corridor redesign against M38's dangerous-intersection redesign. Capped below Close by a sourced miss: the Nov 2025 budget cut crosswalks (−$64K) and traffic signals (−$50K), eliminated the $4.7M Government Street Refresh for 2026 and deferred the multi-modal corridors to 2027. No adaptive-signal programme — the City's 47 detection and 15 monitoring cameras are not adaptive control; no Vision Zero audit or 50%-by-2030 target; no E&N or Westshore rapid-transit endorsement; no automated-speed-enforcement site nominations. M39 struck 1 Sep 2026 — the Dec 2024 unanimous 30/40 km/h vote is not scored.

cells.what: walking and transit the City controls
cells.quote: Council approved 24/7 dedicated bus lanes on Douglas between Hillside and Herald, removing 73 time-limited parking spaces (16 May 2024) — buses are 3% of traffic and 40% of people moved — and the 2026 budget she adopted carries $1.1M to expand accessible sidewalks and pathways, $836,000 for new and upgraded crossings, and $508,000 to replace and widen sidewalks.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: named annual allocations for walking and for transit priority, which is what M20b and M23b ask the City to fund from its own envelope. No published sidewalk-gap inventory, no maximum-crossing-spacing standard, no 1.0 m/s pedestrian clearance rule, no published annual City transit position or Transit Commission voting record. Her only 2026 transportation sentence — “We need to reimagine how we deliver and manage transportation” — names no goal and no instrument: a Mention, not resolved up.

cells.quote: City released a “Guide on Compliance” for the Accessible B.C.
cells.why: Act with the Accessibility Advisory Committee, citing that 40% of residents identify as having disabilities — a guide, not M25b's 24-month audit, dedicated remediation capital line, four-year curb-cut-and-audible-signal programme, or advisory committee with delegated review authority. No Alto quote. On washrooms: 7 City washrooms already operate 24 hours and 13 more dawn-to-dusk — but no council decision, no Alto statement, and nothing approaching M24b's one-per-500-metres downtown standard or real-time status feed.

cells.quote: The 2026 budget she adopted carries $15 million for road restoration and rehabilitation — about seven kilometres of paving — and $44.7 million to rehabilitate underground water, stormwater and sewer mains, and she voted to cancel the Centennial Square revitalization: “I don't think it's ready to advance at this time.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: a funded maintenance-and-renewal-first capital programme, plus a refusal to advance a new build, which is M25's sequencing logic. Capped below Close by a sourced miss: she was named YES, 7–2, on cutting the infrastructure envelope $5.5M → $4M (paving and parks) six weeks earlier. No 7-day report-to-fix pothole standard and no published quarterly road-condition reporting — the two things M25 actually asks for.

cells.quote: Of the 12 community-safety actions, one was a $220,000 City match of provincial CSTEP funding to VicPD, and the Neighbour Network business-safety pilot launched on the 700 block of Fort St in Sept 2025 with City matching.
cells.why: That is coordination and a police top-up, not M28b's capped per-premises reimbursement for private security hours, glazing and sharps servicing in FOI-validated high-exposure zones, and there is no sunset or renewal test. Quote in the coverage is the DVBA's, not hers; no council tally located. Shown, not scored.

cells.what: VicPD funding + regional review (convene-and-publish; no binding other force)
cells.quote: (And) please let us do regional policing.
cells.why: Commits × comparable — she convened it: Victoria, Esquimalt, Oak Bay and Saanich sent joint letters to the Solicitor General on 14 Jul and 6 Aug 2025 seeking talks on a regional service, which she described as noting “our collective interest in examining the future of police services in our communities, while ensuring that any future regional police force maintains excellent services in each municipality”; Minister Krieger replied she is “open to the discussion.” Alto also sits on the Local Government Policing Modernization Roundtable. That is M29b's convene-and-ask without its 18-month time-box, its costed review, or its duty to publish the offer and any refusal. On M29: Esquimalt's share is 13.67% under the 2014 agreement, Esquimalt opted out in Aug 2022, the agreement was extended only to end-2025, and the Police Board voted unanimously on 16 Jun 2026 to appeal the City's budget — no renegotiated service-consumption formula exists. Record supports, not a second mark: named opposed to the 5–4 cut from four new officers to two, 3 Mar 2026. Binding another municipality's force is not claimed, so not scored as Disagrees.

cells.what: safety dashboard, published enforcement record, crime target
cells.quote: We have managed to look comprehensively at what we need to do in the long term around investing upstream to try and minimize the decline of individuals who are vulnerable into places where they cannot recover.
cells.why: Commits × neither: continuing the Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan and reporting it to committee is not M31's weekly dashboard, not M31b's quarterly enforcement record with disputed / upheld / cancelled / paid outcomes, not M31c's restatement of every commitment with legal authority, lead body, timeline, target and cost, and there is no 15%-by-2030 crime target. The op-ed's spend breakdown is money in, not outcomes out — and it carries its mark on row 26. Distinct sentence from row 6, same meeting.

cells.quote: This is all a manifestation of how much we treasure and value the relationship with the Chinese community, how much we understand, how much they've contributed, and that we want to continue that” — at the reopening of the $1.7M restored Gate of Harmonious Interest.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: a completed City heritage restoration against M46's restoration incentive fund and zero tolerance for demolition by neglect. Capped below Close by a sourced miss on her own motion: the Victoria Civic Heritage Trust allocation (~$950K) was paused in the 2026 budget. No Old Town design code (M43), no Victoria Heritage Street Furniture Standard (M44), no cultural-venue designation, right of first refusal or lease-bridge fund (M46b). Launch Mention, context only: “we have to reimagine what heritage is.”

cells.quote: Named YES on cancelling the Centennial Square revitalization, 4 Dec 2025, with more than $700K already spent; $2M of Growing Communities funding redirected to Royal Athletic Park and Crystal Pool on her amendment — “A future council may not have to settle.” Centennial Square full renewal is one of M45c's three named signature-project candidates, and the $4.7M Government Street Refresh — M45b's corridor — was removed from 2026. No pedestrianisation pilot, no Bastion Square scheme, no signature-project shortlist, no referendum commitment. Contradicts no 2026 promise, so shown and not scored.
Hanging-basket budget halved, −$130K, in the 2026 draft budget; the parks share of the $5.5M→$4M infrastructure cut is used on row 30.
cells.why: No waterfront walkway gap-closure programme (M47), no heritage or ornamental lighting extended to midnight (M48), no Parks horticulture restoration, Beacon Hill five-year plan or free-seedling programme (M49). “Protecting parks” sits in the Victoria Buzz second-term list that also contains regional policing, already scored on row 33 — one sentence, one measure.

cells.what: culture, sport, and the arts funding floor
cells.quote: Victoria at Dusk is a celebration of creativity and connection. By activating public spaces and showcasing local talent, we're creating a vibrant downtown experience that supports businesses and brings people together during the winter season,” and CityVibe, 200+ free summer events.
cells.why: Commits × same instrument — M51 is “activate outdoor spaces for year-round use”, and a winter plus summer activation programme is that measure. Capped below Close by a sourced miss: $1.5M was pulled from Royal Athletic Park for the safety plan (2 Jul 2025) against M52's “restore the Royal Athletic Park enhancement budget”, and Major Community Initiatives was halved $200,350→$100,000. No published arts and culture funding floor with a 6-of-9 protection (M50b), no extended evening or Sunday hours for civic cultural spaces (M50).

cells.quote: Service reviews ($1.58M) removed from the 2026 financial plan, 21 Nov 2025, in the package of budget reductions.
cells.why: No zero-based cycle, no three-part jurisdiction / outcomes / duplication test on grants over $50K, no rotating service-area schedule, and no core-services or line-by-line review at any point 2022–26 — searched and confirmed absent. Her vote on that specific line is not itemised in the press opened this pass, so shown and not scored. Budget sentences are scored on rows 13–14.

cells.quote: The City deployed AI without a standard: virtual assistant “Vic” (24/7), Permit Finder and expanded eApply launched 6 Jul 2026, and no public AI register, human-in-the-loop rule, disclosure-by-default policy, privacy impact assessment standard or vendor-training prohibition was located. The 15 Jul 2026 CRD data-centre motion was brought by Caradonna and Thompson, not Alto. Absence of a policy is Record, not Opposed, so shown and not scored.

cells.what: local-tech procurement, open data, Wi-Fi, EV charging
cells.quote: The Purchasing Policy, revised July 2024, carries social procurement and a CRD-local preference below $75,000 — M55's family, but pre-dating the term in substance and adopted administratively, with no innovation-pilot framework and no Canadian-server rule.
cells.why: Open data policy dates to 2011. EV charging: fee moved to $0.35/kWh from 1 Mar 2025, 220+ Level 2 chargers citywide; $3.9M was booked for EV charging in the 2023 budget. No free public Wi-Fi commitment and no 2026 sentence on any of it.

cells.quote: The Climate Leadership Plan update and the new Climate Change Adaptation Plan are still in draft: engagement closed 11 Oct 2024 and the council presentation is scheduled for Fall 2026 — that is, no adoption vote exists in this entire term.
cells.why: The 2026 budget carries $2.3M to advance the low-carbon fleet. No district-energy feasibility study of any kind, no seismic or unreinforced-masonry retrofit policy despite the City's own 2017 finding that a major quake could severely damage ~40% of structures, and no published Climate Friendly Homes uptake figure. Her only climate quote is 2024, not 2026, so it cannot score. This is the weakest-evidenced topic on the card.

cells.what: trees, mode share, ecosystems, emergency preparedness
cells.quote: Canopy cover is 30% across ~150,000 trees and the City says it is still “developing tree canopy targets” — so no 35% target and no 5,000-tree commitment exists; the last cited planting figure is 500 trees in 2020. Stormwater is funded at scale: $44.7M for underground water, stormwater and sewer mains in the 2026 budget, which carries its mark on row 30. Extreme heat: misting stations expanding from 13 to 22 for 2026 on a $42,700 FCM grant — staff quote, not hers. Emergency Preparedness Week release, 4 May 2026, carries no mayor quote. No mode-share target; the transportation
cells.why: Mention sits on row 28.

cells.quote: Crystal Pool assent vote, 8 Feb 2025: 58.71% yes to borrow up to $168.9M over 20 years, 21.18% turnout of 73,409 eligible — the City used M77's instrument once, on one project, and the Program says that project “continues as voted.” A one-off precedent is not a general $25M threshold, there is no five-step sequence, and no material-change or renotification rule — the only related governance change was the 2024 Delegation Bylaw, which reduced public hearings to align with provincial housing statutes (8–1, Alto in the majority).
cells.why: No 2026 sentence proposing any of the three.

cells.quote: Code of Conduct for Council Members Bylaw No. 23-058, adopted 26 Oct 2023 and signed by her, establishes an arm's-length independent investigator — three-year term, selected by unanimous council vote, with the mayor appointing an ad hoc investigator if none exists.
cells.why: Commits × comparable: an external investigator with jurisdiction over council conduct does part of M79b's work. Capped below Close by two sourced misses: the bylaw rejects complaints filed within 90 days before an election and leaves the final determination with Council rather than an independent office; and on the MNP governance report, the 3 Aug 2023 motion declined two recommendations (5.1.4 and 5.5.5) and no public implementation tracker was ever published. On M79's feedback loop: the Dowler Place process — “I take responsibility for a process that could have been better, and will be better going forward” — with no 60-day consultation-response rule adopted.

cells.quote: Named OPPOSED, 5–3, to the 25% council pay increase, 14 Mar 2024 — “It is never appropriate for any agency, ever, under any circumstances to vote itself a raise, either individually or collectively” — and on the revised bylaw, “It wasn't that I don't support the changes. I do. It was that I don't support any part of it taking effect before the next election,” which is M79f's rule in substance.
cells.why: Commits × same instrument on M79f. Capped below Close by a sourced miss running the other way: the City introduced a $10 FOI application fee effective 1 March 2026, where M79e is to waive it. Also silent: no published mandate letter or quarterly portfolio scorecard (M79c), no lobbyist registry for development files (M79d). Counter-context: she was among the six who defeated the Nov 2025 motion to cap future council pay to CPI — a different instrument, not in the Program.

cells.what: neighbourhoods, language access, Local Area Plans
cells.quote: She moved the March 2026 budget package that added $100K back to My Great Neighbourhood grants, alongside $250K for the Burnside Gorge safety hub and $100K for the rent bank.
cells.why: Commits × same instrument — M80 is “expand My Great Neighbourhood and Local Champions” inside the existing grant lines. Capped below Close by a sourced miss: her own council had cut that grant line $152K → $100K in the Nov 2025 budget, so the March motion restores what it removed. No plain-language or official-language access standard (M80b), and no two-Local-Area-Plans-per-year programme — the Local Area Plan programme status could not be sourced at all (M80c).

cells.what: community surveys, turnout and ballot access
cells.quote: The City ran its annual “Have Your Say” engagement on the 2026 draft budget, 7 Jan 2026 — a budget consultation, not M82's statistically valid annual survey across all 12 neighbourhoods with results published by neighbourhood within 90 days and one attributable service change per year. No advance-voting expansion, no voting-where-people-are commitment, no mail-ballot broadening, no turnout target, no post-election turnout report. Counter-context on public access: named YES 7–2 to cut council speakers from five minutes to three, maximum six per meeting, 3 Aug 2023.

cells.what: Saanich amalgamation (one line, not the whole topic)
cells.quote: In my view, we have no choice but to honour that commitment and to respect the work and the citizens who now have an opportunity to express their views on what happens next.” Named YES, 5–4, to put “Do you support Saanich and Victoria becoming one municipality?” on the 17 Oct ballot, 25 Jun 2026 (opposed: Caradonna, Hammond, Gardiner, Thompson).
cells.why: Commits × comparable: she did not re-run the Assembly, and she and Saanich's mayor did request a provincially authorized binding referendum in Oct 2025 — two of M81's four steps. Capped below Close by a sourced miss: Minister Boyle's 20 Apr 2026 letter declined pending the financial, transitional and First Nations analysis, and Alto's answer was “It's up to the province to determine if further work is needed, and to undertake that work if they require it” — a refusal of the one step M81 makes the City's own, commissioning that analysis jointly with Saanich on a published timeline.
